core_rule: Say Celan cleanly and distinctly. The language balances firmness and flow, avoiding swallowed syllables, silent letters, and tonal drift.
why_it_matters: This gives the learner the overall sound ethic of the language before individual letters or rules start to matter.

core_rule: The five vowels stay open and clear: A as ah, E as eh, I as ee, O as oh, U as oo.
why_it_matters: These are the first sound anchors a new reader needs in order to pronounce most Celan words with confidence.
example_1_english: A in Azan lands as ah.
example_2_english: Pelagae lets the open vowels ring through each syllable.

core_rule: Consonants provide structure and grounding. K, T, S, and R appear often and help give Celan its clear, shaped feel.
why_it_matters: This helps learners hear why Celan sounds firm without becoming heavy.
example_1_english: The opening k-r cluster stays crisp and defined.
example_2_english: The s and final r keep the word light but shaped.

core_rule: When fused roots create a harsh or clumsy consonant cluster, Celan may insert a smoothing vowel, usually a, to keep the word flowing.
why_it_matters: This explains why some compounds feel softened, why some stay harsh, and why culture can shape how the same word is spoken.
example_1_english: A harsh cluster is smoothed for easier flow.
example_2_english: The same build may stay harsh or be smoothed depending on voice and style.

unit_title: The Core Idea: Action Comes First
core_rule: In Celan, what is happening arrives before who is doing it. The language centers the action itself.
why_it_matters: This gives the learner the mental shift they need before reading or building any sentence.
example_1_english: The action arrives before the actor: I go to the water.
example_2_english: The event is framed before the people inside it: I love you.

core_rule: A standard Celan sentence begins with the verb, followed by the subject, and then the object or destination.
why_it_matters: This is the baseline sentence skeleton. Many later rules depend on this order feeling natural.

core_rule: Questions place ra at the front of the sentence. Commands place va at the front of the sentence.
why_it_matters: These signposts frame the sentence immediately, so the listener knows whether they are hearing a question or an instruction before the action unfolds.

core_rule: To negate a sentence, place ver directly before the verb. In a negative question, ver sits between ra and the verb.
why_it_matters: This shows how Celan handles refusal, absence, and contradiction without changing the overall sentence shape.
example_1_english: I do not go to the water.

core_rule: Use rath to introduce an if-clause. The rest of the sentence then carries the condition through normal Celan structure.
why_it_matters: This lets the learner move beyond direct statements into hypothetical, dependent, and contingent thought.
example_1_celan: Rath var ser, nor-var I dren.
example_1_english: If the friend goes, I will go to the water.
example_2_celan: Rath Ya var dren, nor-var I shena.
example_2_english: If you go to the water, I will bring coinage.

core_rule: Celan words often grow from compact roots that carry a core idea. New words are built by extending that root rather than by abandoning it.
why_it_matters: This gives the learner the central word-building habit of the language: meaning grows outward from a seed instead of arriving as a random new form.

core_rule: To make a new concept, Celan fuses roots together into one word. The primary idea comes first, and the refining idea comes second.
why_it_matters: This shows how Celan builds new meanings by combining known parts instead of inventing wholly separate vocabulary for every concept.
example_2_english: Earth + sky -> horizon / place where earth meets sky.

core_rule: Pluralization is usually simple: add -in after a consonant-final word and -n after a vowel-final word.
why_it_matters: This gives the learner one of the most practical formation rules in the language and shows how number is marked without changing the root entirely.

core_rule: Celan uses prefixes and suffixes to shift a root into a new grammatical job or a more specific meaning.
why_it_matters: This is how the learner moves from a root to a working verb, place word, descriptive form, or expanded concept.

core_rule: The suffix -eth gives a word the sense of having the quality or essence of something. It can also support more elevated or ritualized forms.
why_it_matters: This helps the learner see how Celan turns core ideas into descriptive qualities without leaving the original concept behind.

core_rule: Celan distinguishes speaker, listener, and others through a compact pronoun system, with singular and plural forms.
why_it_matters: This gives the learner the people-markers needed to place action and relation clearly inside a sentence.
related_terms: I; Ya; La; Ilin; Yalin; Lalin

core_rule: Basic possession is shown by placing the pronoun before the possessed noun, sometimes with the linking particle -ka where needed.
why_it_matters: This gives the learner the simplest way to say my, your, our, and their before moving into deeper relational belonging.

core_rule: Celan distinguishes between direct possession and bonded relation. Ian handles clear personal possession, while -esh marks a deeper connected-to bond.
why_it_matters: This matters because the language does not treat ownership and relationship as the same kind of belonging. Use Ian for something directly yours; use -esh when the point is relationship, attachment, or bonded belonging.
example_2_english: Bonded relation wording: the man connected to me.

core_rule: Prepositions do major structural work in Celan. They mark direction, accompaniment, origin, absence, elevation, and position.
why_it_matters: This helps the learner understand how relation is built in clauses without depending on heavy case marking.
related_terms: Var; Ser; Thal; Ka; An; Nor; Esh; Morl

unit_title: Space and Time: An and Nor
core_rule: An is used for physical location, while Nor is used for time or temporal setting.
why_it_matters: This keeps Celan from blurring place and time into one small English-style preposition.
example_2_english: I go at the appointed time / in time-setting.

unit_title: Case Marking by Order and Particles
core_rule: Celan relies mostly on word order and prepositions for clarity, using particles such as -ka as light linking markers rather than building a heavy case system.
why_it_matters: This helps the learner understand that relation in Celan is usually shown structurally rather than through dense noun endings.

core_rule: Celan builds larger numbers from a compact base set and a small set of scaling prefixes.
why_it_matters: This lets the learner see number as a buildable system instead of a long memorized list.
related_terms: Unar; Del; Tenar; Hek-; Mel-; Fen-

core_rule: Numbers above the base set are built by placing the larger unit first and then adding the next part after it.
why_it_matters: This shows the learner that addition is often built directly into the number phrase itself.

core_rule: Subtraction uses Ven between the two number expressions to mark what is being taken away.
why_it_matters: This gives the learner the visible signal for mathematical subtraction instead of making them infer it from position alone.

core_rule: Celan generally relies on context rather than fixed articles like a or the. Quantifiers appear before the noun they modify.
why_it_matters: This helps the learner avoid forcing English article habits into Celan while still describing amount or scope when needed.
example_1_english: Many breads / much bread, depending on context.

why_it_matters: foundation
example_1_celan: Celan often frames identity through essence and embodied quality rather than through rigid fixed labels alone.
example_1_english: This helps the learner understand why identity language in Celan feels fluid, descriptive, and rooted in qualities rather than only categories.
example_2_english: The neutral person brings strength and balance.
source_ids: A woman embodying neutrality and balance.

teaching_role: Gendered and Neutral Terms in Use
why_it_matters: core system
example_1_celan: Gendered and neutral language in Celan is relational, poetic, and context-sensitive. The same term can shift in force depending on use and setting.
example_1_english: This helps the learner avoid reading these terms as rigid biological labels when the language treats them more dynamically.
example_2_english: My neutral companion flows with the water.
source_ids: A feminine man / a man shaped by feminine qualities.

why_it_matters: advanced use
example_1_celan: Celan allows qualities to be combined when a person is being described through more than one essence or social reading.
example_1_english: This gives the learner a way to understand nuance without forcing identity into one narrow slot.
example_2_english: A man carrying both masculine and feminine qualities.
source_ids: A woman carrying fierce or masculine traits.

why_it_matters: core rule
example_1_celan: Respect is built into the words themselves through honorific particles, titles, and elevated forms rather than left only to tone of voice.
example_1_english: This matters because Celan makes social respect grammatical and visible.
example_2_english: I go to the water, respected friend.
source_ids: Honored guardian, do we proceed to the city's exchange now?

why_it_matters: advanced use
example_1_celan: Social language shifts by culture, setting, and register. Different nations or contexts prefer different tones, titles, and metaphors.
example_1_english: This helps the learner understand that social meaning in Celan is not one flat universal register.
source_ids: I go to the water, respected friend.

core_rule: Capitalization in Celan is meaningful, not automatic. It signals weight, reverence, emphasis, or philosophical significance.
why_it_matters: This helps the learner stop importing English capitalization habits into Celan writing.

core_rule: A normal Celan sentence begins with a lowercase word unless that first word is itself a name, title, or concept that truly calls for capitalization.
why_it_matters: This gives the learner one of the most visible orthographic differences between Celan and English.

core_rule: The first-person singular pronoun I remains capitalized wherever it appears, even when other nearby words stay lowercase.
why_it_matters: This shows that Celan uses visual form to signal the standing of the self without capitalizing everything around it.
example_2_english: I am, in essence, a bird.

why_it_matters: core rule
example_1_celan: Names, nations, titles, and primordial concepts are capitalized because they name something singular, honored, or archetypal rather than merely ordinary.
example_1_english: This helps the learner see that Celan capitalization follows meaning and status rather than sentence position alone.
example_2_english: A nation name and therefore capitalized.
source_ids: An honored title and therefore capitalized.

core_rule: Celan can capitalize an otherwise normal word in poetry or heightened emotion to elevate it into a force, presence, or overwhelming state.
why_it_matters: This gives writers a way to make the page itself carry emotional and philosophical emphasis.
example_2_english: Poetic emphasis: I am Desire itself.

unit_title: Cultural Voice as a Shaping Force
core_rule: Celan is one language across Ohnosha, but it is not one single voice. Nations shape it through metaphor, sound preference, pacing, and social texture.
why_it_matters: This helps the learner understand variation without mistaking national voice for separate grammar systems.
related_terms: Krezthal; Krezathal; Li-Ser; Vael vaar an shara-ya
